record.paper_title: Cyber-Physical Attacks on UAS Networks–Challenges and Open Research Problems
record.original_question: How can real-time, distributed UAS formation-control algorithms minimize topological vulnerability to targeted jamming while retaining connectivity, especially when attack detection and localization may be unreliable and nodes must reform under mission-critical dynamics?

evidence.quote: An alternative mitigation technique is adaptive control of the topology [13]. In this approach, detection of a jamming attack triggers a reformation process during which the nodes of a UAS network change their positions to retain connectivity. A fundamental assumption of this approach is the ability of the nodes to detect and localize attacks, which may not always be practical. A promising area of further investigation is the problem of minimizing the topological vulnerability to targeted jamming attacks. Development of real-time and distributed formation control techniques that consider this optimization problem may lead to highly efficient techniques for ensuring dynamic resilience of mission-critical UAS networks.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a network of $n$ mobile agents (e.g., unmanned aerial vehicles) with positions $x_i(t) \in \mathbb{R}^3$ evolving in continuous time. At each time $t$, the communication graph $G(t) = (V, E(t))$ is determined by a proximity rule: $(i,j) \in E(t)$ iff $\|x_i(t) - x_j(t)\| \le R$, for a fixed communication range $R > 0$. An adversary may carry out a targeted jamming attack at time $t$ by selecting a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ of $k$ jammer locations (with $k$ fixed) which disables every edge $(i,j)$ such that the segment $[x_i, x_j]$ (or one of its endpoints) lies within distance $\rho$ of $S$. Define the topological vulnerability of a configuration $X = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ to $k$-targeted jamming as
$$V_k(X) = \max_{S:\, |S|=k} \, \big[ c(G(X)) - c(G(X) \setminus E_S) \big],$$
where $c(\cdot)$ is a connectivity measure (for instance, the algebraic connectivity $\lambda_2$ of the graph Laplacian, or an indicator of connectedness) and $E_S$ is the set of edges disabled by jammers placed at $S$.

Design a distributed feedback control law
$$\dot x_i(t) = u_i\big(\{x_j(t) : j \in N_i(t)\}, \, \hat z_i(t)\big),$$
where $N_i(t)$ is agent $i$'s current neighborhood and $\hat z_i(t)$ is a (possibly noisy or unavailable) local estimate of attack detection/localization information, such that the resulting closed-loop trajectory $X(t)$ satisfies, while completing a prescribed mission task (e.g., tracking a reference centroid trajectory and maintaining a desired formation up to permutation):

(i) the graph $G(t)$ remains connected for all $t \ge 0$;
(ii) $V_k(X(t))$ is minimized (or kept below a prescribed threshold) in real time;
(iii) the law uses only local information and does not assume reliable global detection or localization of jammers.

Provide such an algorithm together with provable guarantees on connectivity preservation and on the minimization (or bounded suboptimality) of topological vulnerability $V_k$, or prove that no such distributed law with the stated information constraints can simultaneously achieve (i)–(iii).
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of designing real-time distributed formation-control algorithms that provably minimize topological vulnerability to targeted jamming under unreliable attack detection appears to remain open. Related work addresses resilient consensus, connectivity maintenance, and reactive topology reformation, but a distributed formulation with provable optimality of vulnerability under unreliable detection has not been established as a complete solution.
